newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour demands progress on building society law.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour demands progress on building society law.

text.p: Planned legislation for Britain's building societies should be pushed through before it is disrupted by approaching elections, the opposition Labour Party said on Tuesday.

"Unless the government makes an announcement this week, the Building Societies Bill will not be able to complete its stages before the general election," said Shadow Economic Secretary Mike O'Brien. "This will be a blow to the industry."
The government put forward proposed new laws for home lenders in December. Effectively, they would water down building societies' immunity from takeover if they converted into banks.

If the bill was passed, a building society would forfeit its five-year immunity from takeover if it became a bank and then took over another financial institution. But the new law would also remove restrictions on the activities of building societies which wish to retain their mutual status.

The Building Societies Association echoed Labour's calls for the bill to be pushed through. "It is a sensible piece of legislation which will allow societies the flexibility to react to the changing needs and demands of their members," said BSA director-general Adrian Coles.

Labour's O'Brien said there was plenty of parliamentary time before the election, which must be held in the next three months, for the bill to progress. Prime Minister John Major has said May 1 is his preferred date.

"The House rose early last week because of lack of business," O'Brien said. "John Major is focused on the election. He is ignoring the public interest in creating a level playing field so that mutuals can compete."
A host of building societies are converting into banks, quoted on the stock exchange, in the summer.
The Halifax, Woolwich, Alliance & Leicester and Northern Rock Building Societies will all shed their mutual status while the Bristol and West Building Society will be bought by Bank of Ireland.
But others, such as the Nationwide Building Society is determined to remain a mutual, i.e. owned by its customers.
"The government has declared its commitment to the building society industry as a valuable part of the financial infrastructure and I now call on them to back up this claim," Coles said.
"I would urge the government to accept the support being offered by the Labour Party to find parliamentary time to enact this bill."
